# Your one and only setup

You haven't installed anything, and you're not going to. So when this book
tells you to run some code, what runs it?

Not your laptop. You open a web page, and Google starts a Linux machine that
belongs to your account for as long as you're using it. What you type goes up.
The answers come back down. That machine is a computer you'll never touch, and
it costs nothing beyond a Google account.

## Your first cell

Open `colab.research.google.com` and make a new notebook. You'll get a page
with one empty box and a small round button to its left. Click inside the box
and type this, to find out whether the machine will answer.

``` {.python}
print("hello")
```

Press the round button, or hold Shift and press Enter. The answer lands
directly underneath the box you typed in.

``` {.default .output}
hello
```

The first run of a session is slow, because Google is starting your machine
while you wait. Every run after that is fast.

::: {.check}
`hello` should be sitting under the box, on its own. A `[1]` should have
appeared where the round button was. If a ring is still turning there instead,
the machine hasn't finished starting, and the number arrives when it does.
:::

Nothing else on that page matters yet, and the labels on it are not stable.

::: {.asof}
Checked against the live Colab interface on 2 August 2026. Google renames these
buttons every so often. Three things are always there: a box you type into,
something you press to run it, and a menu called Runtime.
:::

## What the parts are called

The box you typed in is a [cell]{.term def="One box in a notebook, holding code or text. Cells run one at a time, in whatever order you click."}. A notebook is a stack of cells, and nothing
forces you to run them top to bottom.

The machine underneath is the [runtime]{.term def="The remote machine that runs your cells. It holds every variable you have made."}. It holds your variables, it's separate from the page in
front of you, and it can die while the page sits there looking healthy.

The bracketed number beside a cell is a counter. It records which run this was,
not which cell this is. Run the top cell, then the one below it, then the top
one again. The top now reads `[3]` and the one below still reads `[2]`. That
counter is your only record of the order things really happened in.

### The notebook remembers

Here's the part that causes more confusion later than anything else in this
book. A variable made in one cell is still sitting there in the next one.

``` {.python}
sequence = "ATGGCC"
print(len(sequence))
```

``` {.default .output}
6
```

``` {.python}
print(sequence.count("G"))
```

``` {.default .output}
2
```

No value was handed from the first cell to the second. The second can see
`sequence` because both ran inside the same runtime, which has held that value
since the first cell finished. Count the G characters in `ATGGCC` yourself and
you'll get 2.

## Four voices

A beginner sees red text and calls it an error. Somebody who has done this a
while looks at the same screen and asks who's speaking. Four things can
interrupt you here, and only one of them is Python.

### Python is talking

Type a name you never made into a cell, then run it.

``` {.python}
print(sequnce)
```

``` {.default .output}
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
NameError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
----> 1 print(sequnce)

NameError: name 'sequnce' is not defined
```

Your screen carries one more line, between the class name and the arrow, naming
a file Colab built out of your cell. It's machine-generated, it changes every
run, and it's left out above because it means nothing.

Two marks identify Python. There's a line of your own code with an arrow
pointing straight at it, and there's a class name, `NameError`, at the top and
again at the bottom. Read the last line first. It's the only line written for a
person.

### The runtime is talking

Ask the machine to hold more data than it has room for and the session dies.
What comes back has a different shape:

``` {.default .output}
Your session crashed after using all available RAM.
```

No line number. No filename. No name out of your own code, and no exception
class. Those absences are the tell. The message is about the machine, and your
code goes unmentioned because your code isn't what failed. Restart the session
and load less: one chromosome instead of the whole genome.

A runtime also disconnects on its own after a stretch of inactivity, and
everything it held goes with it. The notebook text survives because it's saved
elsewhere, but the variables don't.

### A website is talking

Later chapters send you to NCBI and other database sites, where you fill in a
form and press a button. When one refuses you, the page comes back with your
form still on screen and a colored strip near the box you filled in. It
complains about a field, and it can't name a line of code, because you never
wrote any.

The wording on those strips changes with every redesign, so this book won't
print one. The shape doesn't change. Your input is still on screen and the
complaint points at part of it. Fix the input and press the button again.

### The network says nothing at all

The fourth voice has no words: you press run and nothing happens. The ring
keeps turning, no output appears, and no message arrives.

Silence usually means the cell is working. The other thing it can mean is that
something inside the cell is waiting on a connection that isn't coming back.
Neither announces itself, which makes this the one voice you diagnose by
waiting. A cell that normally takes seconds and touches the internet is worth
stopping and running again once it passes a minute.

Naming the speaker first is worth more than any single fix in this chapter. Get
it right and you're looking at one line of your own code instead of at
everything.

## Where your notebooks live

Colab keeps your notebooks in Google Drive and saves them as you work.

This book's notebooks aren't in your Drive. Colab will open one from the
repository Chapter 3 names and run every cell in it, but it can't write your
changes back there. Save a copy into Drive first, from the File menu, and after
that you're editing your own file.

## Running cells in the wrong order

Colab won't make you work down the page in order, and that freedom has a price.

::: {.trap}
Run a cell, edit it, then run the cell below without re-running the one you
edited. The runtime still holds the value from before your edit. The code on
the page and the value in memory now disagree, and the page is what you'll
read. Nothing errors. You'll get a number, it'll look reasonable, and it'll
answer a question you stopped asking ten minutes ago.
:::

Restart and run all is the cure. The Runtime menu has an item that throws your
machine away and runs every cell from the top of a clean one. Google has
labeled it two different ways over the years, so look for the words restart
and run rather than a fixed phrase.

That's the only way to find out whether a notebook works, so do it before you
believe a result and again before you show one to anybody. Chapter 26 turns it
into a rule.

## The one install in this book

Nothing after this chapter asks you to install anything, with one exception.
Chapter 17 opens with the line `!pip install biopython`, typed into a cell like
any other code. A fresh Colab session won't remember it, so you'll run it again
every session, and that's the system working.

itself. If a cell higher up printed `MISSING` or `NOT INSTALLED`, write down
which one and carry on: that's the book's problem to fix, not yours.

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="The page keeps asking you to sign in and will not open a notebook"}
Colab needs a Google account, because a browser with nobody signed in has
nowhere to put your work. Sign in, then open the notebook again. A school or
workplace account can be blocked from Colab entirely by whoever administers it,
and a personal account is the way around that.
:::

::: {.errfix err="Every variable has vanished and the numbers beside your cells are gone"}
The runtime disconnected, which Colab does after a stretch with nobody touching
it, and the replacement is empty. Use restart and run all and let it work back
down the page.
:::

::: {.errfix err="Colab will not save your changes"}
You're working in a notebook you don't own, which is what happens when you open
one straight from a repository. Take the File menu item that saves a copy in
Drive and edit the copy. On a school-managed account, sign into a personal
Google account first and put the copy there. Every notebook here runs the same
on either one.
:::
:::

::: {.checkpoint}
- Run a cell in Colab and read what lands in the output area
- Name the four voices, and say which one points at a line of your own code
- Explain why a variable can outlive the cell that created it
- Predict what a notebook prints when its cells are run out of order
- Restart a runtime and run every cell from the top
:::
